title: How do you answer a market sizing question step by step?
description: How many, how big, how much. The structure earns the points, not the final number.
hook: Answer a market sizing question in six steps: clarify exactly what you are sizing, say a rough guess, choose to build from buyers or sellers, multiply through a short chain of round assumptions, check the result from a second angle, and land a rounded answer with the assumption that drives it. Nobody expects you to know how many piano tuners work in Chicago. The interviewer wants to watch you build an estimate from things you do know, and check that it makes sense.

  • Step 5: Check from a second angle

What the interviewer is testing

Market sizing questions ("How many...?", "How big is the market for...?") turn up on their own, as a warm-up, or in the middle of a bigger case such as market entry. The real number barely matters. Interviewers score three things: whether your structure is logical and complete, whether your assumptions are sensible and stated out loud, and whether you check your answer and say what it means. A clear estimate that is 30% off beats a lucky guess with no reasoning every time.

Step 1: Clarify what you are sizing

Spend 20 to 30 seconds pinning down the question. Four things matter:

  • Units or value? Number of chargers, or dollars spent on them?
  • Geography. Which country or city?
  • Time period. Sold per year, or the total in use today? This is the difference between a flow and a stock, and mixing them is the most common error in sizing.
  • Scope. Consumers, businesses or both? New only, or second-hand too?

"Home EV chargers installed in the UK per year, in units and dollars" is a very different question from "EV chargers in the UK". If the estimate sits inside a case, also ask what decision it informs, because that tells you how precise you need to be.

Step 2: Say a rough guess

Before any maths, give an order of magnitude: "My instinct is a few hundred thousand a year." It shows judgement, and it gives you something to check against. If your calculation lands at 30 million, you know to look for a dropped zero or a wrong assumption.

Step 3: Choose buyers or sellers

  • Demand side, or top-down: start from a population and filter it. People → households → share with a driveway → share buying an EV this year.
  • Supply side, or bottom-up: start from a unit of supply. Chargers one installer fits a week × number of installers.

Start from whichever side you can estimate with more confidence, and keep the other for your check. Consumer purchases usually suit the demand side. Markets limited by capacity, or with few countable sellers, suit the supply side. The buyers' side versus sellers' side quick tip has a checklist for each.

Step 4: Build the chain

Write the formula before the numbers, then fill it in one step at a time, saying each assumption and why. Three habits make this clean:

  • Round hard. 68M, not 69.3M. Say that you are rounding.
  • Segment only where it matters. Split urban and rural, or heavy and light users, if they behave very differently. Do not split for the sake of it.
  • Write units on every line. People, households, purchases, dollars. It stops you multiplying the wrong things.

Also ask whether something limits supply, such as the number of installers, shelf space or seats. Sometimes the limiting factor is the real answer.

Step 5: Check from a second angle

Recompute the number another way: from the other side, as a per-person or per-household figure, or against a fact you know. If the two land within about 20% of each other, you can be confident. If they do not, that is useful too (see below).

Step 6: Land the answer

Give a rounded figure or a range, name the assumption that drives it, and say what it means: "About $10M a year. The share of owners using a paid workshop is the assumption I would test first. For a client opening a new workshop, that suggests a market big enough for a few more players."

A worked example: bike repairs in one city

How big is the market for paid bike repairs in a city of 800,000 people?

Clarify: value per year, workshop repairs only (not bikes or parts bought online). Guess: around $10M.

Demand side:

  1. Residents: 800,000.
  2. Share who own a bike: 25% → 200,000 owners.
  3. Share who use a paid workshop in a year: 60% → 120,000.
  4. Visits each: 1.5 → 180,000 repair visits a year.
  5. Average bill: $55 → 180,000 × $55 = $9.9M a year.

Supply-side check: 40 workshops × 5 mechanics × 4 repairs per mechanic per day × 220 working days = 176,000 visits. That is within about 2% of the demand estimate. You can say "about $10M a year" with confidence, and name the share of owners who use a workshop as the assumption to test.

These are illustrative assumptions for practice, not data about a real city.

When your two methods disagree

Suppose the workshop count had given only 90,000 visits, half the demand figure. That is not embarrassing. It is the most interesting moment in the question. Say what could explain the gap:

  • You assumed too many visits per owner, or too high a share using workshops.
  • Many owners fix their own bikes.
  • The workshop count misses mobile mechanics and bike shops that do repairs on the side.

Then say which method you trust more for this question. If you are sizing the potential need for repairs, the demand side is more relevant. If you are sizing what the industry sells today, observable capacity is the better anchor.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'll size this from owners and check it against workshop capacity. 800,000 people, a quarter with a bike, 60% of them using a workshop 1.5 times a year, is 180,000 visits. At $55 each, that's about $10 million. Forty workshops with five mechanics doing four repairs a day gives a similar number of visits. The share using workshops is the assumption I'd test."

A weak answer recites the multiplication with no clarifying question, no guess and no check, and ends on "$9,900,000" as if it were precise.

Common mistakes

  • Stock versus flow. Bikes owned is a stock. Repairs a year is a flow. Read the question's time period.
  • Fake precision. Round the inputs and the answer.
  • Silent assumptions. If you do not say an assumption, the interviewer cannot agree with it, and you get no credit for it.
  • No sanity check. One method can be wrong in a way you cannot see from inside it.
  • Stopping at the number. Say what it means for the client.

Check yourself

1. What earns most of the points in a market sizing question?

Show the answer

A clear, logical structure with stated, sensible assumptions and a sanity check. Interviewers know you cannot know the true number. They score your logic and judgement, not your accuracy.

2. Why say a rough guess before calculating?

Show the answer

It shows judgement and gives you a built-in check. If your calculation lands far from your guess, you know to re-check an assumption or a zero.

3. Estimate how many cups of coffee London cafés sell on a weekday. Give yourself two minutes, out loud.

Show the answer

Guess: a few million. Build: about 9M residents, of whom roughly 7M are adults, plus about 1M commuters and tourists, so 8M adults. Assume 30% buy a café coffee, 1.5 cups each: 8M × 30% × 1.5 = 3.6M cups. Check: about 14,000 outlets averaging around 250 cups a day gives a similar figure.
